originalGroup.material:
A correction in the school paper

Our school newspaper published a report about the swimming team last month. On the next morning, a team member ____1____ (notice) that one result was wrong. The article said her team had finished second, but it had actually finished third.

The editor thanked her ____2____ pointing it out. He checked the official results before changing anything. The team member was right, and the error had come from an early version of the writer's notes.

At first, the editor wanted to replace the number ____3____ (quiet). Our teacher suggested adding a short correction note instead. Readers ____4____ had already seen the wrong version needed to know what had changed.

The note explained the mistake without blaming the student who reported it. It also gave the correct result. The team was disappointed about not finishing second, but its members preferred an accurate report to ____5____ false success.

The corrected page ____6____ (share) with the team that afternoon. Several students wrote back to say thank you. The editor kept a copy of both ____7____ (version) in the newspaper's records, clearly marking which one had been corrected.

Before ____8____ (publish) the next sports report, the writers checked their notes against the final results. The extra step took a little time, but it was ____9____ (easy) than explaining another avoidable error. The first mistake had not made ____10____ (they) newspaper useless. It had shown where the checking process needed to improve.

Two sides of a balance

In science class, we used a simple balance to compare objects. Our teacher put a small bag on one side and asked us ____1____ (find) objects that would balance it on the other. We were not allowed to open the bag yet.

I chose three wooden blocks. The bag's side stayed lower, so I added another block. My partner watched ____2____ (careful) and asked whether the balance had been level before we started. We had forgotten to check.

After ____3____ (remove) everything, we saw that one pan still hung lower. The teacher helped us adjust the equipment. Only then did we begin our comparison again. A fair result needed more ____4____ a confident guess about the objects.

This time, five blocks balanced the bag. Another group used several metal washers instead. Their answer did not disagree with ours simply ____5____ the number of objects was different. The washers and blocks were not the same mass.

We wrote a description ____6____ explained exactly what we had compared. Then the teacher opened the bag. It contained a small toy car, not the stones I had imagined.

The activity was ____7____ (use) because it made us separate two questions: what an object was and how its mass compared with another's. My notebook showed two different ____8____ (result), with the comparison objects named clearly. The balance ____9____ (check) again before the next class used it. We had learned to examine ____10____ (we) starting point as well as the final answer.

Where the rain gauge stood

The school weather club put a rain gauge in the garden and recorded the water collected after each rainy day. For a week, our numbers were much lower than those from a nearby school. We wondered whether our garden ____1____ (receive) less rain.
